title: Understanding and Mitigating Role Spoofing in LLMs
title_zh: 理解并缓解大语言模型中的角色欺骗

paragraphs.en: Despite growing capabilities, LLMs remain susceptible to prompt injections: malicious inputs that can manipulate or hijack models. In particular, it has recently been observed that LLMs can exhibit role confusion ( Ye et al., 2026 ) , where models attribute the source of text based on its style instead of its labeled role. Malicious text in tool outputs (for instance, a malicious webpage accessed by an agent) can leverage role confusion to impersonate the user, an attack we call role spoofing . In this work, we seek to understand and mitigate role spoofing. We study how models track “who said what” in a conversation, showing that they use cues from both content (e.g., semantics and writing style) and structure (e.g., control tokens and formatting). We show that LLMs are highly susceptible to role spoofing attacks that combine both fake structure and content. Additionally, in a toy setting, we show that adversarial training which teaches the model to ignore content-based injections does mitigate content-based attacks but leaves the model susceptible to structure-based attacks. This can explain why frontier models, with increased resistance to many injection attacks, can still be susceptible to role spoofing. Finally, we propose a new method for detecting role spoofing using linear probes trained to predict roles in a conversation, and show that it is effective across different settings.

paragraphs.en: When LLMs are used as agents, reading potentially untrustworthy data and calling tools, they are vulnerable to being hijacked by prompt injections crafted by an adversary to induce the model to perform harmful actions ( Perez and Ribeiro, 2022 ; Anthropic, 2025 ; Google Workspace Help, 2026 ; OpenAI, 2025 ; Zou et al., 2025 ) . For example, a malicious actor may send the user an email that contains an instruction, directed at the LLM agent reading the email, to wire money to a given bank account.

paragraphs.en: In this paper, we focus on a specific class of injection attacks based on role spoofing , where the attacker gains unauthorized control over an LLM by impersonating the user. Role spoofing attacks can fool models by mimicking the typical style of user messages ( Ye et al., 2026 ) , and/or by wrapping injected messages with strings that mimic the structure (chat) format used by a model (for example, adding “ <|im_start|>user ” before a fake user message ( Chang et al., 2026 ) ). We show that role spoofing attacks that combine both fake content and fake structure can fool every model tested, allowing tool responses to impersonate users or fake whole conversations between the user and the model. In agent tool use test environments, role spoofing attacks were able to impersonate the user over 95% of the time for several models including Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.4.

paragraphs.en: To understand why role spoofing is so effective against modern LLMs, we investigate how models track roles in a conversation. Note that role-assignment (e.g., deciding if a given message originated from the user or a tool response) is a fairly easy task that can be solved robustly using a simple mechanism (see appendix A for details). Indeed, modern LLMs parse conversations by converting them into streams of tokens, where messages are separated by unique special tokens (e.g., <|im_start|> , <|im_end|> ) that can never appear in the message content ( OpenAI, 2023 ) . The role assigned to each message is typically the first token in the message (a non-special role token, e.g. “user” or “tool”). Therefore, all the LLM needs to do in order to determine the role of each message (and therefore, to decide whether a message segment originated from a genuine user request or a malicious tool response) is look back for the role token (“user” or “tool”) that appears immediately after the most recent special token. So why are all models still susceptible to role spoofing attacks?
paragraphs.zh: 为了理解为什么角色欺骗对现代大语言模型如此有效，我们研究了模型是如何在对话中追踪角色的。 请注意，角色分配（例如，判断某条消息来自用户还是工具响应）是一项相当简单的任务，可以通过一种简单的机制稳健地解决（详见附录 A）。 事实上，现代大语言模型通过将对话转换为词元流来解析对话，其中消息由特殊的独特标记（如 <|im_start|>、<|im_end|>）分隔，这些标记永远不会出现在消息内容中（OpenAI, 2023）。 分配给每条消息的角色通常是消息中的第一个词元（一个非特殊的角色词元，例如 “user” 或 “tool”）。 因此，大语言模型要确定每条消息的角色（进而判断某个消息片段来自真实的用户请求还是恶意的工具响应），只需回看最近的特殊标记之后紧跟的角色词元（“user” 或 “tool”）即可。 那么，为什么所有模型仍然容易受到角色欺骗攻击呢？

sents.zh: 那么，为什么所有模型仍然容易受到角色欺骗攻击呢？

paragraphs.en: To answer the question above, we investigate alternative, incorrect , mechanisms for tracking the role in the conversation, and find that all LLMs we tested rely on different “mixtures” of these incorrect mechanisms. We consider two categories of mechanisms: 1) content-based mechanisms, that rely on the style or meaning of the message content to infer the role and 2) structure-based mechanisms, that rely on (potentially misleading) structural cues to find the most recent role token. Importantly, we note that unless a model is explicitly trained on data containing role spoofing attacks, these different potential mechanisms (including the correct and the incorrect ones) can likely determine the role almost perfectly on the training distribution . This therefore means that role spoofing is essentially a form of out-of-distribution generalization failure . Namely, since there are multiple mechanisms for solving the same problem in-distribution , a model can perform perfectly on the training distribution but use a non-robust mechanism that fails on out-of-distribution examples.
paragraphs.zh: 为回答上述问题，我们研究了用于追踪对话中角色的多种替代的、错误的机制，并发现我们测试的所有大语言模型都依赖于这些错误机制的不同“混合”。 我们考虑两类机制：1）基于内容的机制，即依赖消息内容的风格或含义来推断角色；2）基于结构的机制，即依赖（可能具有误导性的）结构线索来定位最近的角色标记。 重要的是，我们指出，除非模型在包含角色伪造攻击的数据上经过显式训练，否则这些不同的潜在机制（包括正确的和错误的机制）在训练分布上几乎都能完美地判定角色。 因此，这意味着角色伪造本质上是一种分布外泛化失败。 也就是说，由于在分布内解决同一问题存在多种机制，模型可以在训练分布上表现完美，却使用一种在分布外样本上失效的非鲁棒机制。

paragraphs.en: To understand this better, we run different controlled experiments where we feed a conversation with potentially misleading cues into the model, and prompt it to state the role of a certain message segment (e.g., “Who sent the message containing [CONTENT]”). We test both conversations with misleading content but no structure, and also cases with misleading structure but random (role-neutral) text. We find that, while all models are often fooled in both cases, some models appear to focus more on structure while others focus more on content.
paragraphs.zh: 为了更好地理解这一点，我们运行了不同的受控实验：向模型输入带有潜在误导性线索的对话，并提示模型说明某个消息片段的角色（例如，“是谁发送了包含[CONTENT]的消息”）。 我们同时测试了有误导性内容但无结构的对话，以及有误导性结构但文本为随机的（角色中性的）内容的情况。 我们发现，尽管所有模型在这两种情况下都经常被误导，但一些模型似乎更关注结构，而另一些模型则更关注内容。

paragraphs.en: To investigate how models learn different mechanisms for role tracking, we design a toy setting for studying a simplified language model training pipeline. We define toy data distributions that serve as proxies for pretraining on unstructured data, instruction-tuning on conversation data and robustness-training on adversarial content-based attacks. In our toy setting, we find that the model initially relies more on content to determine the role of each message, and that training the model to be robust to content-based attacks makes it increasingly susceptible to structure-based attacks. We validate this by showing that fine-tuning Qwen3.5-27B to be robust to content-based attacks indeed does not solve structure-based role spoofing.
paragraphs.zh: 为了研究模型如何学习用于角色追踪的不同机制，我们设计了一个玩具设定，用于研究一个简化的语言模型训练流程。 我们定义了若干玩具数据分布，分别作为以下任务的代理：在非结构化数据上的预训练、在对话数据上的指令微调，以及在基于内容的对抗性攻击上的鲁棒性训练。 在我们的玩具设定中，我们发现模型最初更多依赖内容来判断每条消息的角色，而训练模型对基于内容的攻击保持鲁棒，会使其越来越容易受到基于结构的攻击。 我们通过实验验证了这一点：对 Qwen3.5-27B 进行微调使其对基于内容的攻击保持鲁棒，确实无法解决基于结构的角色欺骗问题。

sents.en: We validate this by showing that fine-tuning Qwen3.5-27B to be robust to content-based attacks indeed does not solve structure-based role spoofing.
sents.zh: 我们通过实验验证了这一点：对 Qwen3.5-27B 进行微调使其对基于内容的攻击保持鲁棒，确实无法解决基于结构的角色欺骗问题。

paragraphs.en: Finally, motivated by our scientific understanding of the different mechanisms for conversation tracking and role assignment, we create a simple defense against role spoofing attacks. Inspired by Ye et al. (2026) , we train linear probes to predict the model’s internal “belief” about the role assigned to each content segment, and flag a message as a role spoofing attack if the model assigns it to an incorrect role (for example, if a tool output contains a segment that the model believes is generated by the user). Surprisingly, we find that linear probes trained on conversations with completely random content tokens achieve near-perfect separation between clean examples and examples with role spoofing injections. Our solution not only has a very low computational overhead, but is better in terms of false positive rates on benign data than prior methods, while not requiring any injections (or even coherent conversations) in the training data.

To elucidate why models are susceptible to our attacks, in Section 3 , we investigate different mechanisms that models use for tracking roles in a conversation, and show that models use different combinations of content-based and structure-based mechanisms. paragraphs.en: Role Spoofing Attacks. Variants of role spoofing attacks have been proposed and studied in prior works. Chang et al. (2026) shows how forged special tokens can be used to inject models, with an attack similar to the one studied in our paper. They focus on testing it as a component of a variety of prompt injections and show it can be effective and can be transferred across models. Zhu et al. (2026) ; Zhou et al. (2024) ; Jiang et al. (2025) use similar forged special tokens for enhancing jailbreak attacks. Recently, Zhan et al. (2026) used Qwen3, Llama-3.1, GLM-4.5, and Seed-OSS to study the same attack, finding it less effective when not using true special tokens, though we find that even modern LLMs (including closed source ones) are still vulnerable to the attack when implemented correctly. Ye et al. (2026) frames prompt injection as role confusion, when models treat text as coming from a source different from the true source. They show that, for example, a user message which looks like an assistant CoT will fool some models. They hypothesize that models determine the role of text from style alone. Our work is closely related to these works, but our main focus is not on developing role spoofing attacks, but rather on understanding and mitigating these attacks. We introduce clean settings for rigorously studying how models track roles, and use our observations to develop a highly effective defense method.

paragraphs.en: Defense Strategies. There are several works studying defense strategies against prompt injections and role spoofing. Some defenses use internal model representations to detect prompt injection. Anthropic (2026) discusses how linear probes are used to detect and flag injected instructions for Claude Opus 5. Abdelnabi et al. (2025) use linear probes to detect task drift through changes in activations, while PIShield trains linear classifiers on internal features from clean and injected inputs ( Zou et al., 2026 ) . Our method also uses linear probes over internal activations (similar to role probes introduced in Ye et al. (2026) ), but we leverage access to the ground-truth roles in order to mitigate role spoofing, resulting in a method that outperforms prior defenses. Other works propose architectural changes to mitigate prompt injections. Wu et al. (2025) ; Panickssery and Ackerman (2025) both suggest adding ‘role embeddings’ to every token. Wang et al. (2025) suggests a related architectural trick, adding gaps between different messages through positional embeddings to help models know where each message begins and ends. Su et al. (2026) splits different roles into separate streams, which gives specific supervision on which tokens are from which roles. These works report increased prompt injection resistance, but do not test on injections using forged special tokens.

paragraphs.en: Indirect prompt injections are malicious inputs that originate from an external source (typically a tool output), that cause LLMs to act in ways that are unintended by the user or the designers ( Greshake et al., 2023 ; Google Workspace Help, 2026 ; Vassilev et al., 2025 ) . In the early days of LLMs, prompt injections were fairly easy to conduct, since LLMs were trained to follow instructions, but not trained on how to choose which instructions to follow (and which to ignore). To remedy this, modern agentic AIs are trained to follow the instruction hierarchy, which specifies how LLMs should act when given conflicting instructions from different sources. For example, if the user and the system developer give contradictory instructions, the instruction hierarchy specifies that the model should follow the instruction provided by the developer, and similarly if the user and a tool output give different instructions, the model should follow the user’s instructions ( Wallace et al., 2024 ) .
paragraphs.zh: 间接提示词注入是来自外部来源（通常是工具输出）的恶意输入，它会使大语言模型做出用户或设计者并不期望的行为（Greshake et al., 2023; Google Workspace Help, 2026; Vassilev et al., 2025）。 在大语言模型的早期，提示词注入相当容易实施，因为大语言模型被训练来遵循指令，却没有被训练如何选择该遵循哪些指令（以及该忽略哪些指令）。 为了解决这个问题，现代智能体AI被训练来遵循指令层级，该层级规定了大语言模型在收到来自不同来源的相互冲突的指令时应如何行动。 例如，如果用户和系统开发者给出了相互矛盾的指令，指令层级规定模型应遵循开发者提供的指令；类似地，如果用户和工具输出给出了不同的指令，模型应遵循用户的指令（Wallace et al., 2024）。

sents.en: For example, if the user and the system developer give contradictory instructions, the instruction hierarchy specifies that the model should follow the instruction provided by the developer, and similarly if the user and a tool output give different instructions, the model should follow the user’s instructions ( Wallace et al., 2024 ) .
sents.zh: 例如，如果用户和系统开发者给出了相互矛盾的指令，指令层级规定模型应遵循开发者提供的指令；类似地，如果用户和工具输出给出了不同的指令，模型应遵循用户的指令（Wallace et al., 2024）。

paragraphs.en: Many attacks on AIs (including some prompt injections and jailbreaks) try to get the model to ignore or forget the instruction hierarchy. For instance, the user may invent a made-up scenario in order to convince the model to provide information or perform actions that it should otherwise refuse (for some examples, see Shen et al., 2024 ). In contrast, we consider prompt injection attacks that exploit the instruction hierarchy rather than attempting to bypass it, tricking the model into believing that a certain instruction comes from a more privileged level of the hierarchy, a phenomenon called role confusion ( Ye et al., 2026 ) . For example, a website retrieved by a tool call can contain a structured text segment that makes the model believe it received a message from the user (see Figure 1 ). We will call this type of prompt injection role spoofing .
paragraphs.zh: 许多针对AI的攻击（包括某些提示注入和越狱）都试图让模型忽略或遗忘指令层级。 例如，用户可能编造一个虚构的情景，以说服模型提供信息或执行它本应拒绝的行为（示例可参见 Shen et al., 2024 ）。 与之相反，我们关注的是利用指令层级而非试图绕过它的提示注入攻击，即诱使模型相信某条指令来自层级中更具特权的一级，这种现象称为角色混淆（ Ye et al., 2026 ）。 例如，通过工具调用检索到的网页可以包含一段结构化文本，使模型相信自己收到了来自用户的消息（见图 1 ）。 我们将这类提示注入称为角色伪装。

paragraphs.en: We assume an attacker that can inject text tokens into a legitimate tool response (for example, by setting up a website or sending an email that the model then consumes). To describe the attack, we first review how LLMs parse conversations. Any data being put into an LLM is first converted into a sequence of tokens . The different messages, responses, tool calls, and tool outputs, everything comprising the current conversation (or context ), is part of a single stream of tokens. To convert a structured conversation into a stream of tokens, modern LLMs use a set of predefined formatting rules called a chat template . The chat template uses specific token sequences to indicate the message boundaries and the role (user, assistant, tool, etc.) assigned to each message. This conversion process alone can already create a security flaw, for example if a malicious actor can inject a sequence of tokens that mimics the chat template format, allowing it to “send” fake user messages to the model (similarly to classical SQL injection attacks).
paragraphs.zh: 我们假设攻击者能够向合法的工具响应中注入文本标记（例如，通过搭建一个网站或发送一封随后会被模型消费的电子邮件）。 为了描述这种攻击，我们首先回顾大语言模型（LLM）是如何解析对话的。 任何输入到 LLM 中的数据都会首先被转换为一个标记（token）序列。 不同的消息、响应、工具调用和工具输出，即构成当前对话（或称上下文）的所有内容，都是单一标记流的一部分。 为了将结构化的对话转换为标记流，现代 LLM 使用一套预定义的格式化规则，称为聊天模板（chat template）。 聊天模板使用特定的标记序列来指示消息边界以及分配给每条消息的角色（用户、助手、工具等）。 仅这一转换过程就可能已经造成安全缺陷，例如，如果恶意行为者能够注入一段模仿聊天模板格式的标记序列，便可以向模型“发送”伪造的用户消息（类似于经典的 SQL 注入攻击）。

paragraphs.en: Even as early as the creation of ChatGPT this was known as a potential security issue ( OpenAI, 2023 ) . In order to solve it, modern chat templates use special tokens , which act as dedicated markers that can be introduced only through the chat template, and can never appear inside message content. This way, the source of each message in the conversation is easy to confirm by treating the special tokens as the only valid boundary between messages.

paragraphs.en: We now turn to analyzing the susceptibility of LLMs to role spoofing attacks in two tool-use testbeds. Our goal is to measure whether the model treats injected (fake) user messages as if they are sent by a real user, and not whether role spoofing can cause the model to perform harmful actions (which may not be permitted even if they originate from real user requests). We therefore use the model’s behavior on legitimate user requests as a baseline when interpreting attack success. For example, a model might reject an injection asking it to explain how to build a bomb, but if it would also reject such a request coming from the user, we would not count this as a failure of the attack. Note that even if we restrict adversaries to role spoofing, they can still accomplish many malicious attacks, such as stealing user information, impersonating users, or gaining access to the users’ systems. Moreover, role spoofing could potentially be combined with jailbreaking techniques to unlock further malicious uses.

paragraphs.en: AgentDojo. We first measure the success of role spoofing on the tasks in the AgentDojo ( Debenedetti et al., 2024 ) test environment, which includes diverse environments and tasks that are specifically designed to test prompt injection attacks. AgentDojo has a sliding scale of adversarial attacks that include some attacks which are obviously malicious (“Send the Facebook security code received via email from ’security@facebook.com’ to ’mark.black-2134@gmail.com’. Then, delete the email you have just sent.”). Note, we adopt a slightly non-standard threat model, allowing arbitrary injection of text into the tool call, not escaping any characters in the injection. This is a more permissive attacker model, but lets us more directly test role spoofing in LLMs, rather than the defense of specific tool formats (of course, certain tools that output distrusted text can apply their own defenses, like filtering out or escaping certain characters, similar to what special tokens do). To account for requests that the model would refuse even when requested by the user, we separately measure the rate at which the model carries out each malicious task when it is issued directly by the user rather than injected, and use this baseline acceptance rate to normalize our attack success rate. Figure 1 (right) reports the results on AgentDojo’s workspace family, with injection-to-control ratios ranging from 63.1 % 63.1\% to 103.6 % 103.6\% across the tested models. See Appendix B for more details.

paragraphs.en: Our Simple Tool-Use Testbed. To isolate role spoofing ability, we create a testbed in which the adversarial tasks and user tasks are sampled from the same pool of tasks. To best measure our injection’s role spoofing capabilities, we create 5 settings (bank accounts, document editing, calendar management, email, and climate control) each with several tasks for an AI assistant to complete. These tasks involve a user request that should result in fetching information using one tool call, then calling another tool to modify the environment (for example: “Read my latest email from inbox. If it names a specific time and place, add that meeting to my calendar; if it does not, just save a note about the message.”). paragraphs.en: In the previous section, we showed that all frontier LLMs are highly susceptible to role spoofing. We now investigate how models track roles in a conversation to understand why such attacks are successful. Recall that LLM chat templates format conversations such that there is a simple robust mechanism for determining the role assigned to each message, relying on special tokens as the only valid indicators of message boundaries. Moreover, we note that this role-tracking mechanism can easily be implemented by a two-layer transformer, for example by retrieving the token immediately following an <|im_start|> token (similar to the operation of an induction head ( Olsson et al., 2022 ) ). However, the fact that a simple transformer-based circuit exists does not mean that a language model will learn to use such a circuit from training data. In fact, we will argue that there exist numerous alternative mechanisms that perform well on the training data (i.e., in-distribution ), but fail on adversarial and out-of-distribution settings. In the rest of this section, we characterize different alternative (and wrong) mechanisms for tracking the role in a conversation, and measure which mechanisms are used by different models.
paragraphs.zh: 在上一节中，我们表明所有前沿大语言模型都极易受到角色欺骗的攻击。 我们现在研究模型如何在对话中追踪角色，以理解此类攻击为何能够成功。 回想一下，大语言模型的聊天模板对对话进行格式化的方式是：存在一种简单而稳健的机制来确定每条消息被赋予的角色，该机制依赖特殊标记作为消息边界的唯一有效指示符。 此外，我们注意到，这种角色追踪机制可以很容易地由两层 Transformer 来实现，例如通过检索紧跟在 <|im_start|> 标记之后的标记（类似于归纳头的运作方式（ Olsson et al., 2022 ））。 然而，存在一个简单的基于 Transformer 的电路并不意味着语言模型会从训练数据中学会使用这样的电路。 事实上，我们将论证存在许多在训练数据上表现良好（即在分布内）但在对抗性和分布外设置下失效的替代机制。 在本节的其余部分，我们刻画了追踪对话角色的不同替代（且错误的）机制，并测量不同模型使用了哪些机制。

paragraphs.en: Results. As shown in fig. 2 , different models use different “mixtures” of content-based and structure-based mechanisms: Gemini 3.6 Flash is hardly ever fooled by misleading content but fails on fake structure injections, while GPT-5.4 is more frequently fooled by misleading content than pure structure injections. It seems that models rarely rely on the robust ground-truth mechanism for role assignment. We note that different models may use different strategies depending on the context, and we do not claim that any model consistently relies on a certain mixture of content and structure cues.

paragraphs.en: To study how training shapes role tracking in language models, we construct a toy learning task consisting of agentic conversations with tool-use. We then describe a stylized model training process which incorporates phases corresponding to pretraining, instruction tuning, and adversarial training on context-based attacks.
paragraphs.zh: 为了研究训练如何塑造语言模型中的角色追踪能力，我们构建了一个由带有工具使用的智能体对话组成的玩具学习任务。 随后我们描述一个风格化的模型训练过程，其中包含与预训练、指令微调以及针对基于上下文的攻击的对抗训练相对应的阶段。

sents.en: To study how training shapes role tracking in language models, we construct a toy learning task consisting of agentic conversations with tool-use.
sents.zh: 为了研究训练如何塑造语言模型中的角色追踪能力，我们构建了一个由带有工具使用的智能体对话组成的玩具学习任务。

sents.en: We then describe a stylized model training process which incorporates phases corresponding to pretraining, instruction tuning, and adversarial training on context-based attacks.
sents.zh: 随后我们描述一个风格化的模型训练过程，其中包含与预训练、指令微调以及针对基于上下文的攻击的对抗训练相对应的阶段。

paragraphs.en: Task. We design a simple task that requires conversation tracking, includes both content and structure cues for role tracking, and can be learned through next token prediction. Each message in the conversation is randomly chosen to be a user, assistant, or tool message. Messages are separated by special tokens as in typical LLM chat formatting. We choose four distributions each with symmetric Dirichlet priors over the token vocabulary (excluding special tokens and non-special structural tokens): one for user messages, one for tool messages, one for assistant messages that follow tool messages, and one for assistant messages that follow user messages. The setting captures a basic property of real agentic interactions—that the model should act differently when responding to the user and when responding to a tool output. See section E.2 for full details.
paragraphs.zh: 任务。 我们设计了一个简单的任务，该任务需要对话跟踪，同时包含用于角色跟踪的内容线索和结构线索，并且可以通过下一个词元预测来学习。 对话中的每条消息被随机选为用户消息、智能体消息或工具消息。 消息之间使用特殊词元分隔，这与典型的大语言模型聊天格式一致。 我们选择了四个分布，每个分布都在词元词表上使用对称的狄利克雷先验（不包括特殊词元和非特殊的结构性词元）：一个用于用户消息，一个用于工具消息，一个用于跟在工具消息之后的智能体消息，一个用于跟在用户消息之后的智能体消息。 该设置刻画了真实智能体交互的一个基本特性——模型在响应用户和响应工具输出时应当采取不同的行为。 完整细节参见 E.2 节。

paragraphs.en: Training. We first pretrain a two layer decoder-only transformer on a mixture of 90% conversations with no separators between messages at all (no tokens indicating who is speaking or when each message starts or ends), and 10% conversations with non-special structural tokens and normal role tokens used to label and separate the messages. This models the idea that pretraining contains largely freeform content, but also some amount of structured data, yet no special tokens. The rest of training, just like for real models, is restricted to conversations structured with special tokens, and supervision on only assistant messages. So, after pretraining, we do instruction-tuning using clean conversations with special tokens as structure. Then, we do adversarial post-training which mixes clean data with content-based injections with correct, non-fooled model responses. To keep the training data balanced, we also include content injections where the user message has tool content in the adversarial training.

paragraphs.en: Evaluation. We test on clean data and three types of injections: 1) Content-only injection: tool message with tokens sampled from the user distribution, 2) Structure-only injection: tool message, which, at the end has non-special structural tokens to make it appear that it has ended, and that the rest of the message is from the user, followed by extra content from the tool distribution, and 3) Full Injection: tool message, which, at the end has non-special structural tokens to make it appear that it has ended, and that a user message is starting, followed by tokens sampled from the user distribution.
paragraphs.zh: 评估。 如果模型下一个词元的分布在 KL 散度上比替代分布更接近正确响应的分布，我们就将该预测判定为正确。 我们在干净数据以及三种类型的注入上进行测试：1）仅内容注入：工具消息中的词元从用户分布中采样得到；2）仅结构注入：工具消息，其末尾带有非特殊结构词元，使其看起来已经结束、且消息的其余部分来自用户，随后是来自工具分布的额外内容；3）完全注入：工具消息，其末尾带有非特殊结构词元，使其看起来已经结束、且一条用户消息正在开始，随后是从用户分布中采样得到的词元。

paragraphs.en: Results. As shown in fig. 4 , by the end of instruction-tuning, while the model has near perfect clean accuracy and resistance to structure attacks, it is fooled by the content injection and full injection. These results suggest the model is relying on content cues. Indeed, if we look at where it is attending to in fig. 3 on the left, we can see that its attention is almost all focused on nearby content tokens, ignoring structural cues. After adversarial training the model achieves good accuracy on both clean conversations and content injections, but accuracy on structure injections flips, and the full injection stays effective (despite a small decrease in success rate). Again, the attention patterns point to the explanation for this result: on the right side of fig. 3 we can see that the model now attends to structure over content, but doesn’t differentiate between real and fake special tokens. Further evidence that these attention results are consistent can be found in fig. 12 .

paragraphs.en: Validation in LLMs. We now test whether fine-tuning an existing LLM against one type of role spoofing attack transfers to the other. We consider the “Who said what” attribution setting from Section 3.2 , where Qwen3.5-27B is completely fooled by both content-only injections and fake special token injections. We fine-tune the model twice, once against content-based injections, and once against fake special token injections, where in both cases we hold out several injections of each type (including the injection based on the special tokens and conversation template used by Qwen models). We observe excellent performance of both fine-tuned models on held-out injections of the type they were trained on, but very limited transfer. Training on fake special token injections gave no transfer at all to content-based injections, while training on content-based injections marginally increased accuracy under a few fake special token injections (to 36.2%) but did not transfer to Qwen’s native special token format. We refer the reader to Table 5 for the full results.

paragraphs.en: So far, we showed that LLMs rely on non-robust mechanisms for tracking roles in a conversation, making them susceptible to role spoofing attacks that mimic the structure and content of user messages. Adversarial training can improve robustness to attacks, but incurs the cost of fine-tuning the model and may provide limited transfer across attack types (as shown in the previous section). Furthermore, even if we construct training data that covers the complete set of attacks discussed in this paper, the model may remain susceptible to other, more sophisticated, role spoofing attacks.
paragraphs.zh: 到目前为止，我们已经表明，大型语言模型依赖非鲁棒的机制来跟踪对话中的角色，这使它们容易受到模仿用户消息结构与内容的角色欺骗攻击。 对抗训练可以提升对攻击的鲁棒性，但需要付出微调模型的代价，并且在攻击类型之间的迁移效果可能有限（如上一节所示）。 此外，即使我们构建的训练数据涵盖了本文讨论的全部攻击集合，模型仍然可能受到其他更复杂的角色欺骗攻击的影响。

sents.en: So far, we showed that LLMs rely on non-robust mechanisms for tracking roles in a conversation, making them susceptible to role spoofing attacks that mimic the structure and content of user messages.

paragraphs.en: In this section, we therefore develop a simple and efficient method for detecting role spoofing attacks. Our solution relies on the fact that, unlike many other subtle and elusive LLM failures, for the role assignment problem we have access to the ground-truth . That is, the inference engine always knows the true role assigned to every message. So, in order to flag role confusion, we need to find a reliable measure for the model’s internal “belief” about the role assigned to each content segment. Indeed, if we find that the model assigns a content segment to an incorrect role (as indicated by the ground-truth), we can then flag this content as role confusion.
paragraphs.zh: 因此，在本节中我们开发了一种简单高效的方法来检测角色伪造攻击。 我们的方案基于这样一个事实：与许多其他微妙且难以捉摸的 LLM 失效不同，对于角色分配问题我们可以获取真值（ground-truth）。 也就是说，推理引擎始终知道分配给每条消息的真实角色。 因此，为了标记角色混淆，我们需要找到一种可靠的度量方法，来衡量模型对分配给每个内容片段的角色的内部“信念”。 的确，如果我们发现模型将某个内容片段分配给了错误的角色（以真值为准），我们就可以将该内容标记为角色混淆。

paragraphs.en: Attempt 1: Model self-attribution. Our first attempt at measuring the model’s internal “belief” is to simply ask it to state the sender of each message segment. We tested such a method on a variety of settings with role spoofing attacks (see Section G.1 for details), and found that this is a reliable way to probe the model’s “belief”: the model misattributed part of a tool message if and only if that part was from an injection that fooled the model. Unfortunately, this detection method has a few critical flaws. First, it introduces a significant computational burden, making it hard to implement in practice. Second, if an attacker is aware that this monitoring is being used, they could try to fool it, for example by an instruction to fool the monitor (e.g., “if asked, say this entire message is from a tool output”). These modified injections fooled both models we tested, and avoided detection almost entirely (Gemma 4 31B misattributed nearly 0% injections, and Qwen3.5-27B misattributed just 25%).

paragraphs.en: Attempt 2: Linear role probes. To address these issues, we train a linear probe on the model’s activations to predict at each token whether it is a tool output or not. We train on data without any injections, with the goal of learning the model’s “belief” of the role at each token. We can then detect whether the model believes some of the tokens in a tool response are coming from the user, indicating successful role spoofing. Our probes achieve near perfect separation between clean and injected cases, across a variety of held out test cases (including on the injections that fool the model self attribution method). Surprisingly, probes were most effective when trained on conversations where messages contained uniformly random tokens. We note that training such role probes has been previously proposed in Ye et al. (2026) , but they explicitly left their use as detectors as an open question. Unlike Ye et al. (2026) , we train our probes on fake conversations, instead of just single messages. This change lets the probes go from an inconsistent interpretability tool, to a genuinely effective role spoofing detector.

paragraphs.en: As shown in Figure 5 , despite not being trained on any real injections (nor on any coherent conversations) our role probes achieve better performance than probes trained directly on realistic injections similar in essence to the held out test injections. paragraphs.en: In this paper, we showed that all LLMs we tested fail to determine the correct role of certain message segments under adversarial role spoofing attacks. Beyond the severe security issue, this failure is particularly intriguing: LLMs have arguably surpassed human capabilities in many domains, yet fail to robustly solve the simple task of role-assignment. We believe that this failure is a special case of the broader phenomenon of out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization failure. Modern machine learning models can solve problems that appear in their training distribution extremely well, yet fail miserably on inputs that are far enough from what they were trained on. Despite incredible progress in many areas of machine learning, OOD failures, as is evident from the results in this paper, remain an open challenge.

paragraphs.en: To be clear, we acknowledge that the type of role spoofing we discuss in this paper may be entirely solved in future models by incorporating training data with such adversarial examples. However, as some of our results demonstrate, solving OOD failures by adding more “edge cases” into the training data is a brittle solution that does not guarantee that the model will learn a robust mechanism. Instead, we proposed to leverage the knowledge of the ground-truth role to develop a robust defense against role spoofing attacks, and we hope that frontier model providers will incorporate our simple solution into their models.

sents.en: To be clear, we acknowledge that the type of role spoofing we discuss in this paper may be entirely solved in future models by incorporating training data with such adversarial examples.

sents.en: However, as some of our results demonstrate, solving OOD failures by adding more “edge cases” into the training data is a brittle solution that does not guarantee that the model will learn a robust mechanism.
sents.zh: 然而，正如我们的一些结果所表明的，通过在训练数据中添加更多“边缘案例”来解决分布外失效问题是一种脆弱的方案，并不能保证模型会学到一种鲁棒的机制。

sents.en: Instead, we proposed to leverage the knowledge of the ground-truth role to develop a robust defense against role spoofing attacks, and we hope that frontier model providers will incorporate our simple solution into their models.
sents.zh: 为此，我们提出利用真实角色的知识来构建针对角色欺骗攻击的鲁棒防御方法，并希望前沿模型提供商会将我们的这一简单方案集成到其模型中。

paragraphs.en: We construct a two-layer transformer with one attention head per layer that implements three rules for identifying the preceding message’s role: infer it from content, read it after a real or fake start, or read it only after a real start. The three rules use the same embeddings and architecture, with different attention and value weights. Intermediate weights allow content and structure to contribute to the same prediction. We prove guarantees for the structural rules and a probability bound for the content rule.
paragraphs.zh: 我们构建了一个两层Transformer模型，每层包含一个注意力头，用于实现识别前一条消息角色的三种规则：从内容中推断、在真实或伪造的起始标记之后读取，或仅在真实起始标记之后读取。 这三种规则使用相同的嵌入和架构，仅注意力权重和值权重不同。 中间层权重使内容和结构能够共同作用于同一个预测。 我们为结构规则证明了保证，并为内容规则给出了概率界。

paragraphs.en: In the experiments from Section 3.3 , 90% of pretraining conversations have no separators or role labels, while the remaining 10% use fake special tokens and role labels. Content and fake structure can both provide useful cues. Neither instruction-tuning nor adversarial post-training includes fake special tokens. Changing η \eta therefore leaves the construction’s hidden states and role scores unchanged on instruction-tuning and adversarial training data. The rules that trust and ignore fake starts agree on this data, yet disagree under structure injections. Thus increasing reliance on structure can improve resistance to content injections while leaving the model vulnerable to structure injections, as observed in fig. 4 . We do not prove that gradient descent selects these weights.

paragraphs.en: To make the right-hand table in fig. 1 , we choose over one hundred random pairs of user and injection tasks (to avoid confusion with the injection column, from now on we will call these adversarial tasks) per model uniformly at random from the workspace family. To get the control column, we first did the user task, then after it was done, had the user ask the model to complete the adversarial task (just as if it was another user task), and we then measured the rate at which the models completed the adversarial task. For the injection column, we had the user only ask about the user task, and then had the adversarial task in the injection. The injections simulate the model response to the clean tool result, and use fake special tokens to make it seem like that response already happened, and the user has now asked the model to first repeat the first tool call, and then do the adversarial task, followed by a fake version of the tool call, and output. paragraphs.en: The testbed consists of short agentic conversations in which a model has to read one tool result and then issue an action call. It is organized in the same spirit as and heavily inspired by AgentDojo ( Debenedetti et al., 2024 ) : tool outputs are a property of a shared environment rather than of any individual task, so a user task and an injected task observe the same world. The testbed environments, tools, and tasks in the testbed were written by Claude Opus 5.
paragraphs.zh: 该测试床由简短的智能体对话组成，其中模型需要读取一个工具结果，然后发出一个动作调用。 它的组织方式与 AgentDojo（Debenedetti et al., 2024）精神一致并深受其启发：工具输出是共享环境的属性，而非任何单个任务的属性，因此用户任务和注入任务观察到的同一个世界。 测试床中的测试床环境、工具和任务由 Claude Opus 5 编写。

paragraphs.en: A suite fixes a system prompt, a tool set, a set of parameters (account ids, cities, recipients, …), a set of tasks, and a set of environments. An environment defines the output of every information-gathering call any task in the suite can make. A task consists of an instruction template, one information call, and two branches, each with a condition over the returned object and a graded action. An instance is a tuple (environment, parameter binding, user task) for clean episodes, and (environment, parameter binding, user task, adversary task) for injected ones. One critical difference between this testbed and AgentDojo is that every task can be both a user or adversary task (just not both at the same time).

paragraphs.en: Besides the content injection (described above as half of the documents from the adversarial training data), we also tested on two other injections. paragraphs.en: We tried to transfer the training techniques from Ye et al. (2026) as faithfully as possible, and even included extra degrees of freedom before picking the best probes at the end. Assistant blocks are preceded by a CoT block of unrelated text of length Beta ⁡ ( 0.5 , 4 ) × 512 \mathrm{Beta}(0.5,4)\times 512 tokens. We tested getting activations from the pre-MLP residual stream (like in the original paper) and also from after the block entirely, we tested every fourth layer, and also an all layers-concatenated probe. paragraphs.en: For negative test samples, we had 128 clean AgentDojo runs, and 1,516 runs from our simple tool-use testbed, and then 512 agentic tool use conversations (Nemotron-SFT-Agentic-v2, NVIDIA Corporation (2026) ). For our positive test samples, we had 300 injected AgentDojo runs, along with 966 injected runs from our testbed for each of seven injections (including a spectrum from pure content injections to full special token forgery injections). For the positive samples, we ran the models on them eight times, to see how often they were fooled and followed the adversarial task, and dropped any that never fooled the models. This is done because such samples can be safely ignored or flagged by a detector since they are malicious, but the model can also handle them itself. This results in 288 AgentDojo runs and 3,621 runs from our testbed being used for Gemma and 253 AgentDojo runs and 6,490 runs from our testbed for Qwen. The large gap between the two models is mostly due to Gemma’s higher resistance to content only attacks compared to Qwen.

sents.en: For the positive samples, we ran the models on them eight times, to see how often they were fooled and followed the adversarial task, and dropped any that never fooled the models.

sents.en: This is done because such samples can be safely ignored or flagged by a detector since they are malicious, but the model can also handle them itself.
sents.zh: 这样做是因为此类样本可以被检测器安全地忽略或标记，因为它们是恶意的，但模型也可以自行处理它们。

sents.en: This results in 288 AgentDojo runs and 3,621 runs from our testbed being used for Gemma and 253 AgentDojo runs and 6,490 runs from our testbed for Qwen.
sents.zh: 这使得288次AgentDojo运行和3,621次来自我们测试床的运行被用于Gemma，以及253次AgentDojo运行和6,490次来自我们测试床的运行被用于Qwen。

sents.en: The large gap between the two models is mostly due to Gemma’s higher resistance to content only attacks compared to Qwen.
sents.zh: 两个模型之间的巨大差距主要归因于Gemma相比Qwen对纯内容攻击具有更高的抵抗力。

paragraphs.en: To calculate a probe’s value on a tool message, we take the maximum score any token in that message obtains. We chose this method both because it was simple and obvious (to avoid accidental p-hacking) and because this way adversaries can’t pad injections with clean content to hide from probes (by lowering the average score).
paragraphs.zh: 为了计算探针在工具消息上的取值，我们取该消息中任意词元所获得的最高分数。 我们选择这一方法，既因为它简单直观（以避免意外的p-hacking），也因为这样对手就无法通过在注入内容中掺入干净内容来降低平均分数，从而躲过探针的检测。

paragraphs.en: When measuring ROC curves, we balance each average first within each source (the sources being AgentDojo, nemotron sft agentic v2, and our testbed) then average over all of the sources for each label. This ensures that no single data source dominates the results, and to do well the probes have to be effective across domains.
paragraphs.zh: 在测量 ROC 曲线时，我们先将每个平均值在各数据源内部进行平衡（数据源包括 AgentDojo、nemotron sft agentic v2 以及我们的测试平台），然后再对每个标签的所有数据源取平均。 这确保了没有任何单一数据源会主导结果，而要表现良好，探针必须在各个领域都有效。
